Record date: 2129-10-03
South Elizabeth Seychelles Hospital INTERNAL MEDICINE DEPARTMENT Location: 4923 Olivia Parkway Suite 217, Lake Jennabury
PATIENT: Lysander Fairfax Phone: 28451903 email:bradleymorgan@example.org DATE OF BIRTH: 1947-05-12 AGE: 80 years
FOLLOW-UP DATE: 10/03/29 FOLLOWED BY: Dr. Emily Carter
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Persistent cough with episodes of wheezing and increased fatigue.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Lysander Fairfax returns for a follow-up appointment two weeks after his last visit. He reports that while he initially experienced some improvement, his symptoms have worsened over the past few days. The cough remains persistent and is now accompanied by occasional sputum production, which he describes as clear. He notes increased wheezing, particularly at night, and has experienced a significant uptick in fatigue, which has limited his ability to engage in daily activities.
The patient has adhered to his medication regimen, including oral furosemide, tapered prednisone, and nebulized albuterol every two hours. However, he expresses concern that the albuterol is not providing the same relief it once did. He denies any chest pain, hemoptysis, or fever but mentions that he has been using his rescue inhaler more frequently than before.
REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General - + increased fatigue, - weight loss, - fever, - chills, - night sweats. Pulmonary - + persistent cough with clear sputum, + increased wheezing, - hemoptysis. Cardiac - no chest pain, - orthopnea, - paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Gastrointestinal - no nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Musculoskeletal - no joint pain. Neurological - no dizziness or headaches.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: - Blood Pressure: 134/78 mmHg - Heart Rate: 82 bpm - Respiratory Rate: 22 breaths/min - Oxygen Saturation: 88% on room air.
General: The patient appears fatigued but is alert and in no acute distress.
HEENT: No nasal flaring; oropharynx clear, no signs of dehydration.
Lungs: Moderate wheezing noted on auscultation, particularly on forced expiration; no crackles present, but prolonged expiration noted.
Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs or gallops; peripheral pulses intact and symmetric.
Extremities: No edema; no tenderness on palpation.
ASSESSMENT
1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation; persistent cough with clear sputum and increased wheezing likely indicating airway inflammation. 2. Congestive heart failure stable; no signs of fluid overload. 3. Increased fatigue likely related to exacerbation of COPD.
PLAN
1. Increase nebulized albuterol frequency to every 1 hour as needed for wheezing; consider the addition of a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) to the regimen for better symptom control. 2. Initiate a short course of oral prednisone at 40 mg daily for 5 days to manage acute exacerbation of COPD, followed by a taper. 3. Continue oral furosemide 40 mg daily; monitor fluid status closely and adjust as necessary. 4. Schedule a follow-up appointment in one week to reassess respiratory symptoms and medication efficacy. 5. Reinforce education on the importance of adhering to the prescribed inhaler regimen and avoiding known triggers, including smoke and allergens.
Mr. Fairfax was encouraged to monitor his symptoms closely and instructed to seek immediate medical attention if he experiences any worsening of his condition, such as increased shortness of breath or chest discomfort.
DISPOSITION
Mr. Fairfax was discharged home with updated medication instructions, including the new prednisone regimen and increased nebulizer use. A follow-up appointment has been scheduled for one week from today to evaluate his response to the adjusted treatment plan.
